source_text: Ergo si Apostolus non arguit in illo propriam voluntatem, quam intellegit nec esse potuisse; pronuntiat utique, nec signum in eo criminis apparere, ea maxime iudicante iustitia, quae non imputat peccatum, nisi a quo liberum est abstinere. Verum non hoc solum tribuisse contentus, addis: Neque nuptias arguit Apostolus, in quantum nuptiae sunt, quae habent a Deo non solum institutionem, verum etiam benedictionem [n46] . Quod per se solum aeque posset ad expugnandum peccatum naturale sufficere; quia, si scit Apostolus, ut scit, non esse nuptias arguendas, ad quarum conciliationem et ministerium et instrumentum pertinet a Deo instituta et benedicta sexuum cum voluptate commixtio; non potest de his diabolica germinare possessio, nec fructus earum reus est, apud eam maxime iustitiam, quae peccatum non imputat, nisi unde liberum est abstinere.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore if the Apostle does not accuse in him a proper will, which he understands could not even have been; he pronounces at any rate that not even a sign of a crime appears in him, that justice especially judging which does not impute sin except from that from which it is free to abstain. But not content to have granted this alone, you add: Nor does the Apostle accuse marriages, insofar as they are marriages, which have from God not only institution but also blessing. Which by itself alone could equally suffice for storming natural sin; because, if the Apostle knows, as he knows, that marriages are not to be accused, to whose conciliation both the ministry and the instrument belong, the mingling of the sexes with pleasure instituted and blessed by God; a diabolical possession cannot germinate from these, nor is their fruit a defendant, before that justice especially which does not impute sin except from that from which it is free to abstain.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere

pass_b_english: If, then, the apostle does not accuse the infant of a personal will, understanding that such a will could not yet have existed, he certainly declares that no sign of guilt appears in the infant. This is especially true when the judge is justice, which imputes no sin except one from which abstention is possible. But, not content to grant this alone, you add: ‘Nor does the apostle accuse marriage, insofar as it is marriage, which has not only its institution but also its blessing from God’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.45). This by itself could equally suffice to overthrow natural sin. For if the apostle knows, as he does know, that marriage is not to be accused, and if the pleasurable union of the sexes, instituted and blessed by God, belongs to marriage as its means and instrument of union, then no possession by the devil can sprout from marriage. Nor is its fruit guilty, especially before that justice which imputes no sin except one from which abstention is possible.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
